description:
Screaming Frog Group Buy is an option to compare if you need the Screaming Frog SEO Spider for technical SEO audits and want to check a lower-cost offer before committing to an annual licence. Start with the work you need to finish. A freelancer fixing broken links on a small WordPress site has different needs from an agency auditing a large store after a migration. Crawl size, software version, exports, and access terms matter as much as the price on the product page.

The SEO Spider is a desktop website crawler. It can help you find broken links, follow redirects, and review titles, headings, and other technical signals across the pages it discovers. Screaming Frog sells its own licences. This SEOGBTools listing is a separate offer, so confirm the current access arrangement and check it against the vendor’s terms before ordering. Do not assume that a group buy offer includes the same licence rights, updates, or features as a direct purchase.

What can you do with Screaming Frog SEO Spider?

A website crawl follows links and records what it finds at each address. Instead of opening hundreds of pages one at a time, you can use the crawl to identify groups that deserve a closer look. For instance, you may find several category pages pointing to a missing policy, repeated titles across products, or old links that reach their destination through a chain of redirects. Open a few examples to verify each pattern before assigning work.

Crawl data also gives you a record to compare after a change. If a team replaces an old menu link, you can check the affected pages and run the same crawl again. If a migration changes many URLs, compare the intended destination with the one that opens. Keep the original report, date, and settings so the next person can reproduce the check without guessing what was included.

A crawl describes what the tool reached under the settings you chose. It does not by itself prove that Google has indexed the pages or that a warning is hurting search performance. Use Search Console URL Inspection for Google's reported view of an important URL you own. For a visitor problem, test the live page directly on the device where someone encountered it.

Plan the first crawl around one job

Pick a site you are authorized to audit. Choose a clear question, such as whether your shop navigation still points to any old product categories. Identify which pages belong in the first pass. A home page and one store section can be enough to test the process before you crawl a larger site. Record the starting address and the URLs that should be included.

Take care with scope. A WooCommerce site can expose many versions of a category through filters, sorting options, or pagination. Decide whether your first job concerns the main category pages or those filtered URLs as well. If the site owner has crawl restrictions or capacity limits, respect them. Check that the crawl is manageable before you scale it across the whole site.

Save the baseline where your access allows. Include the date, website, starting address, relevant settings, and examples of the issue. If you only need to test a small list of known URLs, focus the work on those addresses. A narrowly scoped test is easier to reproduce and can answer a specific question faster than a full audit.

Find and fix broken internal links

Start with error URLs that a visitor could reach. A missing page listed in an old report may have no current internal links, while a link in a product menu can affect many people. Open the source page, find the link a shopper would select, and follow it. Write down the source, link text, and final address. That is the evidence a developer or editor needs to locate the problem.

Consider a store that renamed its delivery policy. If product descriptions still link to the old address, check whether the current policy is the right destination. Update the link in the source template or description, depending on where it comes from. If external sites still refer to the old policy and the new one serves the same purpose, check whether an appropriate redirect should also remain in place.

For a discontinued product, confirm the business decision before redirecting it. A similar model can be a useful destination when it meets the same need. A homepage redirect may leave a shopper unsure where to go. If there is no relevant replacement, remove outdated internal links and make it easy to reach a suitable category through navigation or related products.

Check redirects, canonicals, and page titles

Read the URL report with the site's intended behavior in mind. A redirect from an old address can be useful. A link that sends shoppers through several redirects can usually point directly to the final destination. If two URLs show similar content, compare internal links, sitemap entries, and canonical tags to see which version the site identifies as preferred. Review important examples before changing a shared rule.

If several pages have the same title, check whether they serve different tasks. Two pages for different services should help a searcher tell them apart. A filtered product view may need a different decision from a main category. Review what each URL does and which version you intend to make visible in search. Keep a separate note for tasks that need a developer and tasks a content editor can handle.

Check the outcome on the public page. A title can look correct in WordPress while the live theme generates something different. Open the final URL and verify the title and heading that are actually present. If you are reviewing indexability, check the relevant directives and use Search Console on a small set of high-value URLs rather than assuming every warning has the same cause.

Free SEO Spider versus paid access

The official free version can crawl up to 500 URLs in a single crawl. If you only need to inspect a small public website or learn the basic workflow, try that version first. The official paid licence removes that crawl limit and enables advanced features. Screaming Frog lists options such as saving and reopening crawls, JavaScript rendering, custom extraction, and integrations among the capabilities to compare. See Screaming Frog SEO Spider for the vendor's current details.

A large crawl can still depend on the machine and the site you are auditing. Think about how you will store reports and whether you need to open them later. For a JavaScript-heavy site, check whether the workflow you choose can render what matters on your pages. If you need a particular integration or export for client work, verify it on a small public test before relying on it for a deadline.

Screaming Frog states that its official licences are per user. If you are comparing a discounted offer, ask how access is provided, what it permits, and whether it follows the vendor's licence terms. Confirm the supported version, operating system, available features, update policy, and access period. If those details are unclear and the job depends on them, compare the official licence or test the free version before you pay. The official terms are available at Screaming Frog SEO Spider licence.

What to check before buying discounted access

Check the amount charged at checkout and the period it covers. A short access period can suit a one-time cleanup, while recurring audits may need stable access and the ability to save crawl projects. Compare what you can actually use during that period. A low price has little value if you cannot export the report your client needs or run a crawl big enough to finish the job.

Ask whether you can install the tool on the operating system you use and which version you will receive. Confirm how to get help if activation fails, how the offer handles updates, and whether refunds or replacements are available under the current terms. If your work needs a licensed seat for multiple team members, check the vendor's per-user requirements and compare the full cost for the team.

Test with a public site before entering private client information. A crawl export can contain page URLs, metadata, or other details a client may expect you to keep private. Check the access arrangement and your client agreement before connecting an account or importing protected data. Keep permitted reports in the project folder you control, with the date and settings beside them.

Retest the changes before closing the audit

After the change goes live, open the affected pages and repeat the exact steps that exposed the problem. Follow the corrected links, confirm the intended destination, and look at both mobile and desktop when layout matters. If the issue came from a shared template, check more than one example. A product page with a long title or a different category can expose a problem that a single preview missed.

Rerun the crawl with comparable settings. If the issue count dropped, confirm the relevant pages are still included in the crawl. A lower count can also happen when a section stops being discovered. Compare the scope, not just the final number. Keep one or two examples that show the fix and note any remaining cases separately.

If your next task is a smaller browser-based audit, see SEOptimer Group Buy. For another crawl workflow focused on site structure and internal links, compare Seobility Group Buy. The tools can help with overlapping tasks. Use the report that gives you enough evidence to reproduce the issue and confirm the fix on the pages you own.

A simple audit plan for freelancers and site owners

If this is your first client audit, choose three types of pages: a page that brings leads, a page that helps customers choose, and a page people reach after clicking a key link. Record the final URL for each. Run the crawl, then compare the report with what a signed-out visitor sees. Put confirmed issues into a short task list and explain how the client can verify the fix.

For example, a service site may have old links to a quote form. Start by fixing the links visitors use, then check whether any old address still needs a redirect. Record the result for several representative pages. Once that job is finished, decide whether you need a broader crawl for titles, redirect chains, or site structure. This makes it easier to judge whether a free test meets your needs or paid access would save time.

Frequently asked questions

Is Screaming Frog a browser tool or desktop software?

The official SEO Spider is desktop software. Check the vendor's current system requirements and confirm how the SEOGBTools listing delivers access before ordering. A third-party access arrangement may differ from installing and licensing the software directly.

Is the free version enough for a small site?

It can be enough when your crawl stays within the official limit and you only need the basic checks. If your project requires advanced options or more URLs, compare the paid features you need and test a representative section first.

Can I use Screaming Frog for a site migration?

Yes, a crawl can help record old URLs, inspect where they redirect, and find internal links that still point to old addresses. Build a list of the important URLs and their intended destinations before launch. After launch, verify the redirects and crawl the new site to confirm important pages are discoverable.

Does an SEO Spider crawl prove Google indexed a page?

A crawl shows what the tool found under its settings. Use Search Console to check Google's reported index status for a URL you own. Compare the live page, the crawler's findings, and the date of Google's reported view when the results differ.

What should I confirm before ordering this group buy?

Check licence terms, access duration, operating system, version, support, updates, exports, and any crawl limits. If you need to audit a client site, confirm the setup works with the information you are allowed to use. Choose the option that can complete your actual audit from the first crawl through the final report.
